altruistic

al-troo-ISS-tik -- from Latin alter, 'other': an altruistic person acts for the other person. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Altruistic is unselfish and generous toward others.

Donating a kidney to a stranger is about as altruistic as a person can get.

Example

A student who has been saving all year for new sneakers makes an altruistic choice: quietly handing the money to a classmate whose family lost everything in a fire, and never mentioning it to anyone.

Acting for someone else's good at real cost to yourself, with nothing to gain in return, is what makes the choice altruistic. Unlike 'kind,' which covers any pleasant act, altruistic stresses that your own interest was set aside.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

charitable: Charitable means giving help -- money, food, time -- to people in need, and it often points at organized giving to strangers. Altruistic is about the motive underneath: your own interest set aside entirely. A charitable donor may still enjoy the tax break and the applause; an altruistic one seeks nothing back.

benevolent: Benevolent describes a kindly attitude -- wishing others well and meaning to do good, the way a benevolent ruler treats subjects gently. Altruistic goes past attitude to action and sacrifice: an altruistic act costs you something real for someone else's benefit. Benevolent is warm feeling; altruistic is your own interest set aside.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

selfish: caring only about your own interests

greedy: wanting far more than your share

Where it sits · how little personal gain is sought

generous → altruistic → selfless

generous vs. altruistic: Generous is milder and broader than altruistic -- you can be generous with a big tip and still enjoy the credit, while altruistic suggests you gained nothing at all.

selfless vs. altruistic: Selfless is the strongest word in this family: altruistic describes acting for others' benefit, while selfless suggests your own interests barely entered your mind.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — altru-: other people, somebody else (Italian (altrui), from Latin alter ('other'))

suffix — -ist: one who holds a belief or practice (Greek (-istes), via French)

suffix — -ic: characteristic of (Latin (-icus), from Greek -ikos)

Put it together: The French philosopher Auguste Comte coined altruisme in the 1830s from Italian altrui, 'somebody else,' which traces back to Latin alter, 'other' -- an altruistic person is literally 'other-centered,' from the same root that gives us alternative and alter ego.

Use the root in a new word: alternative: The committee argued for an hour before settling on the alternative.

Altruistic is a compliment, and it usually describes people, motives, or acts -- 'altruistic motives,' 'a purely altruistic gesture.' The matching noun is altruism.
